p1.key: All six hydrogens in benzene are in identical chemical environments, so the 1H NMR spectrum shows one signal.

In CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)CH<sub>3</sub> the second carbon carries four different groups (H, NH<sub>2</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub>, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>), so it is chiral. None of the other compounds has a carbon with four different groups.
In CH3CHClCH3 the two CH3 groups are equivalent (6 H) and there is one CH (1 H): two environments.
C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> (e.g. 1,2-dichloroethene) has cis and trans isomers. The cis form is polar, while in the trans form the bond dipoles cancel, making it non-polar.
I is correctly 2-methylpentane and III is 2,3-dimethylbutane. II is wrongly named: the longest chain has four carbons, so it is 2,2-dimethylbutane.
In C(CH3)4 all 12 H are equivalent, giving one peak. In CH3COOCH3 the two CH3 groups are in different environments (next to C=O or next to O), giving two peaks. Ethanol gives three. I only.
Methoxyethane (an ether, b.p. about 7 °C) has no hydrogen bonding and only weak dipole forces, so it is a gas at 25 °C. Propanone (56 °C), propanal (49 °C) and ethanoic acid (118 °C) are liquids.
(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>COH has two environments: nine equivalent CH<sub>3</sub> protons and one OH proton. Benzene and CH<sub>3</sub>OCH<sub>3</sub> give one peak, and ethanol gives three.
Ethanoic acid (strong H-bonding, forms dimers) > ethanol (H-bonding) > fluoroethane (dipole–dipole) > ethane (London forces only): 4, 3, 2, 1.
In HOCH(CH<sub>3</sub>)COOH (lactic acid) the central carbon carries four different groups (H, OH, CH<sub>3</sub>, COOH), so it is chiral. Glycine's CH<sub>2</sub> carbon has two identical H atoms.
C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>Cl has four structural isomers: 1-chlorobutane, 2-chlorobutane, 1-chloro-2-methylpropane and 2-chloro-2-methylpropane.

In CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CHO, carbon 2 bears H, CH<sub>3</sub>, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub> and CHO: four different groups, so it is chiral. None of the other compounds has a carbon with four different groups.
A broad band near 3300 cm−1 is O—H (hydrogen-bonded), and about 1060 cm−1 is C—O. With no C=O near 1700 cm−1, ketones and acids are ruled out, so the compound is an alkanol.
An amine contains an –NH<sub>2</sub> group bonded to a carbon chain: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> (ethylamine). B is an amide, C a polyamide, D a nitrile.

The spectrum shows two peaks, in a 1 : 3 area ratio, at about 4.4 and 3.3 ppm. CH<sub>3</sub>OH fits: OH (1H) and CH<sub>3</sub>–O (3H). Ethanol would give three peaks; HCHO one peak near 9.7 ppm; HCOOH two peaks near 8 and 11 ppm.

In CH<sub>3</sub>CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)COOH (alanine) the central carbon carries four different groups: H, CH<sub>3</sub>, NH<sub>2</sub> and COOH. In the others, a carbon has two identical groups (2 H, 2 NH<sub>2</sub> or 2 CH<sub>3</sub>).
CH3COOC2H5 has M = 88 (molecular ion). Fragments: C2H5+ = 29, CH3+ = 15, CH3CO+ = 43. No sensible fragment has m/z = 32.

In CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)COOH (lactic acid) the central C carries four different groups: CH<sub>3</sub>, H, OH and COOH, so it is chiral. C has two CH<sub>3</sub>, D has two CH<sub>3</sub>, and A has two H on the same carbon.
(CH3)2CH–CH2–CH3: the two CH3 on the CH are equivalent (1), then CH (2), CH2 (3) and the end CH3 (4): 4 environments.

I is butane, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>. II and III are two ways of writing 2-methylpropane, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CH, the branched isomer of C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>.
p1.flag: duplicate of 2003M paper (identical images and markscheme)

p1.key: In CH<sub>2</sub>BrCHBrCH<sub>3</sub> the middle carbon has four different groups (H, Br, CH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>2</sub>Br), so it is chiral. In A, C and D the middle carbon carries two identical groups.
p1.flag: duplicate of 2003M paper (identical images and markscheme)

p1.key: CH<sub>3</sub>COOCH<sub>3</sub> has two H environments (two different CH<sub>3</sub> groups), so 2 peaks. The others each have three: HCOOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub>OCH<sub>2</sub>CHO and CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH.
p1.flag: duplicate of 2003M paper (identical images and markscheme)

p1.key: Successive members of a homologous series differ by one CH<sub>2</sub> unit. They share the same functional group and general formula but not the same empirical formula.
CH<sub>3</sub>CHBrI has a carbon bonded to four different groups (H, CH<sub>3</sub>, Br, I), so it is chiral. The other compounds have no carbon with four different substituents.
All 12 H atoms in C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub> are equivalent (four identical methyl groups on one carbon), so there is one chemical environment and a single signal.

These are isomers of similar mass. (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>C is the most branched and compact, giving the smallest surface contact and weakest London forces, so the lowest boiling point. The ether is slightly polar.

In 1-chloro-2-methylpentane, C2 carries H, CH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>2</sub>Cl and C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>: four different groups, so it is chiral. In 3-chloropentane and 2-chloro-2-methylpentane two groups on the C–Cl carbon are identical.
Propan-2-ol has three H environments: the six equivalent CH<sub>3</sub> H atoms, the CH, and the OH. Propane and ethane-1,2-diol have two; propan-1-ol has four.

1-Chlorobutane has the same functional group (chloro on C1) and differs from 1-chloropropane by one CH<sub>2</sub>. 1-Chloropropene is unsaturated, 1-bromopropane has a different halogen, and the dichloro compound has two Cl.

Pentane is CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, written in condensed form as CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>: five carbons in a chain. D shows CH<sub>3</sub> groups in the chain, which is not possible.

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO readily breaks at the C–C bond next to C=O to give CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> and CHO<sup>+</sup>, both m/z = 29, so this is the most intense peak. 58 is the molecular ion, which is weak after complete fragmentation.
In CH<sub>3</sub>CHBrCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (2-bromobutane), the C–Br carbon is bonded to two other carbons: secondary. A and C are primary; D is tertiary.
C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub> has five structural isomers: hexane, 2-methylpentane, 3-methylpentane, 2,2-dimethylbutane and 2,3-dimethylbutane.
In CH<sub>3</sub>CHBrCOOH the central carbon carries H, CH<sub>3</sub>, Br and COOH: four different groups, so it is chiral. In B, the central carbon has two identical CH<sub>2</sub>Cl groups.
CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH has three hydrogen environments (CH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>2</sub> and OH), giving three peaks in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1.
In C (2-methylbutan-2-ol) the carbon bearing OH is bonded to three other carbons: tertiary. A and B are primary (CH<sub>2</sub>OH); D is secondary.

The longest chain has five carbons (CH<sub>3</sub>–CH–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>3</sub>) with a methyl group on C2: 2-methylpentane. Names like 1,3-dimethylbutane come from not using the longest chain.
In (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCOCH<sub>3</sub> there are three H environments: the two equivalent CH<sub>3</sub> groups on the CH (6H), the CH (1H) and the CH<sub>3</sub> next to C=O (3H).

A tertiary halogenoalkane has the C–Br carbon bonded to three other carbons. In CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>Br the C–Br carbon carries an ethyl and two methyl groups. A is secondary; B and C are primary.

The longest chain is 6 carbons (through the ethyl group): CH3CH2–C(CH3)2–CH(CH3)–CH2CH3. Numbering for lowest locants gives methyls on C3, C3, C4: 3,3,4-trimethylhexane. C and D do not use the longest chain.
A chiral carbon has four different groups attached. The four CHOH carbons (C2–C5) are chiral; the CHO and CH2OH carbons are not (C1 has a double bond to O, C6 has two H). Answer 4.
CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH3 (2-methylbutane): the two CH3 groups on the CH are equivalent (6H), then CH (1H), CH2 (2H) and the end CH3 (3H): 6 : 1 : 2 : 3.

M⁺ = 58 fits C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O. Peaks at 43 (CH<sub>3</sub>CO⁺, loss of CH<sub>3</sub>) and 15 (CH<sub>3</sub>⁺) fit propanone, CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub>. Propanal would show 29 (CHO⁺ / C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>⁺) and 57 rather than a strong 43.
Aldehydes contain the –CHO group at the end of a chain: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO (propanal). B is a ketone, C a carboxylic acid and D an ester.

A chiral centre needs four different groups. In B (alanine) the central carbon has H, CH<sub>3</sub>, NH<sub>2</sub> and COOH, so it has optical isomers. A has two H atoms, C two CH<sub>3</sub> groups and D two NH<sub>2</sub> groups.

m/z 15 = CH<sub>3</sub>⁺ and 29 = C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>⁺ (or CHO⁺). C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub> has only methyl groups on a central carbon, so it can give CH<sub>3</sub>⁺ but has no ethyl fragment. A, B and D all contain C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>/CHO units.

Butane (I) has 2 H environments (CH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>2</sub>). Propanoic acid (II) has 3 (CH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>2</sub>, OH). (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br (III) has 3 ((CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>, two different CH<sub>2</sub>).

2,3-dichloro-2-methylpentane: a 5-carbon chain with Cl and CH<sub>3</sub> on C2 and Cl on C3: CH<sub>3</sub>CCl(CH<sub>3</sub>)CHClCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>. C would be 2,2-dichloro-3-methylpentane.

In butan-2-ol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, C2 carries H, OH, CH<sub>3</sub> and C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>: four different groups, so it is chiral. C has two CH<sub>3</sub> on the CH; D has two H on the central carbon; A has a C=C.

Mass spectrometry gives the molecular ion peak, i.e. the relative molecular mass, plus fragments. ¹H NMR gives hydrogen environments (not bond lengths), and IR identifies bonds/functional groups, not bond angles.
Hydrogenating CH3CH2CBr=CH2 gives CH3CH2CHBrCH3; C2 carries four different groups (H, Br, CH3, C2H5), so it is chiral. B gives CH3CHBrCH3 and D gives 2-methylbutane, neither chiral. C.
The spectrum has three peaks with areas in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3, so there are three H environments. Ethanol has OH (1), CH2 (2) and CH3 (3). Options A, B and D each have only two environments. C.
For C3H5Cl3, place three Cl on a propane chain: 1,1,1-; 1,1,2-; 1,1,3-; 1,2,2-; and 1,2,3-trichloropropane. That is 5 structural isomers.
Optical activity needs a chiral carbon with four different groups. In CH3CH2CHClCH3, C2 carries H, Cl, CH3 and C2H5. None of the other compounds has a chiral centre. C.
The alcohol part (methanol) gives the first word, 'methyl', and the acid part (propanoic acid, 3 C) gives 'propanoate': CH3CH2COOCH3 is methyl propanoate.

Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but a different arrangement (connectivity) of atoms. A describes isotopes, B describes members of a homologous series, and C is not a definition of isomers.

Classify by the number of carbons attached to the C–OH carbon. In 1 it has three C neighbours: tertiary. In 2 the OH is on a CH2 attached to one carbon: primary. In 3 the C–OH carbon has two C neighbours: secondary.
CH3CH2CONH2 has three carbons including the C=O, and the –CONH2 amide group: propanamide. Ethanamide (B) has only two carbons; propylamine is an amine (–NH2 with no C=O).
Ethanol + butanoic acid (4 C) gives an ester named alcohol part first, 'ethyl', then acid part, 'butanoate': CH3CH2CH2COOCH2CH3, ethyl butanoate. B reverses the two parts.
C2H2Cl2 has 3 isomers: 1,1-dichloroethene, and cis- and trans-1,2-dichloroethene. There is no rotation about the C=C bond, so the cis and trans forms are distinct.
Hexane chain (6 C) with Br on C2 and C3 and a methyl on C3: CH3–CHBr–CBr(CH3)–CH2CH2CH3. B. A has its methyl on C4.
CH3(CH2)2COOCH3: the acid part, CH3CH2CH2COO–, has 4 C (butanoate), and the alcohol part is CH3 (methyl). So it is methyl butanoate.
In CH3CHBrCHBrCH3, C2 and C3 each carry H, Br, CH3 and a –CHBrCH3 group: four different groups. So there are 2 chiral carbons (one stereoisomer is the meso form).
I is pentane, C5H12, and III is 2-methylbutane, also C5H12: same molecular formula, different structure, so they are structural isomers. II is methylpropane, C4H10, which has a different formula. B.
An amide contains –CONH2: CH3CONH2 (ethanamide). A is an ester, C an amine and D an amino acid. B.

1,2-Dichloroethene, ClCH=CHCl, has restricted rotation about the C=C, with different groups on each carbon, so it has cis and trans (geometrical) isomers. 1,2-Dichloroethane has free rotation, and neither compound has a chiral carbon.

Butan-2-ol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, has a carbon bonded to four different groups (H, OH, CH<sub>3</sub>, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>), so it is chiral. None of the other molecules has such a carbon.

X and Z both have H/CH<sub>3</sub> on one carbon and COOH/CH<sub>3</sub> on the other, but with the groups swapped across the double bond, so they are cis–trans isomers. W and Y have different substituents (Y has two H), so they are different compounds.
Propan-2-ol and butan-2-ol are both secondary alcohols differing by one CH<sub>2</sub>, so they belong to the same homologous series. The other pairs contain different functional groups.
An aldehyde has a terminal –CHO group: butanal, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO. A is an alcohol, B a ketone and C an ester.

In 2-chlorobutane, C2 carries four different groups (H, Cl, CH<sub>3</sub>, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>), so it is chiral and optically active. 2-aminoethanoic acid (glycine) has two H atoms on its central carbon, so it is not chiral.
An ester contains –COO– linking two carbon groups: CH<sub>3</sub>COOCH<sub>3</sub> (methyl ethanoate). A is a carboxylic acid, C contains ketone and alcohol groups, D is a dialdehyde.
In 2-iodobutane, C2 is bonded to H, I, CH<sub>3</sub> and C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>, four different groups, so it is chiral. In 3-iodopentane C3 has two identical ethyl groups.

The longest chain including the CN carbon has 3 carbons (propanenitrile, C1 = CN carbon), with two methyl groups on C2: 2,2-dimethylpropanenitrile. The molecule has 5 carbons in total but not in one chain.
p1.flag: nitrile naming not explicitly in 2025 syllabus

p1.key: (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCOCH<sub>3</sub>: the longest chain has 4 carbons with C=O on C2 (lowest locant) and a methyl on C3: 3-methylbutan-2-one. It is a ketone, not an aldehyde.
Methadone has a C=O between two carbons (ketone), two benzene rings, and an N bonded to three carbons with no C=O next to it (a tertiary amine, not an amide). It has no aldehyde or alkene groups.
Butane is non-polar with only London forces. Propan-1-ol and propanoic acid form hydrogen bonds, and 1-bromopropane is polar and has many more electrons, so butane has the lowest boiling point.

In 1-bromo-2-methylbutane, C2 carries H, CH<sub>3</sub>, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub> and CH<sub>2</sub>Br, four different groups, so it is chiral. In 3-bromopentane C3 has two identical ethyl groups; propan-2-ol has two CH<sub>3</sub> groups.
Enantiomers rotate the plane of plane-polarized light by equal amounts in opposite directions; a polarimeter measures this rotation.

The longest chain containing the C=C has 6 carbons, with the double bond at C2 and a methyl group at C4: 4-methylhex-2-ene. The chain carbons on each side of the double bond are on opposite sides, so it is trans. "4-ethylpent" names a chain that is not the longest.

2-chlorobutane, CH<sub>3</sub>CHClCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, has a chiral carbon (C2) bonded to four different groups: H, Cl, CH<sub>3</sub> and C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>. In 3-chloropentane, C3 carries two identical ethyl groups, so it is not chiral.
An alcohol and a carboxylic acid react (esterification) to form an ester. Esters have fruity smells and are used as food flavourings and in perfumes.
p1.flag: uses of esters not explicit in 2025 syllabus

p1.key: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN has 4 carbons including the C of the –C≡N group, so it is butanenitrile. Propanenitrile wrongly leaves out the nitrile carbon.

A geometric isomer of cis-1,2-dichlorocyclobutane is trans-1,2-dichlorocyclobutane: Cl atoms on adjacent carbons but on opposite faces of the ring. A shows this. D is the same cis compound, and B and C are 1,3-isomers.

(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–CO–CH<sub>3</sub> is a ketone with a 4-carbon chain. Numbering to give C=O the lowest number puts it at C2 and both methyls at C3: 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-one. It is not an aldehyde, so C and D are wrong.
C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CONHC<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub> contains two phenyl rings joined by a –CONH– group, which is an amide (a C=O directly bonded to N). It is not a ketone plus an amine.

Esterification: the alcohol supplies the alkyl part (butyl) and the acid supplies the -oate part (ethanoate), so the product is butyl ethanoate, CH<sub>3</sub>COOC<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>. Ethyl butanoate (C) has the parts reversed.

(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> has a 5-carbon chain. Numbering from the end nearest the OH puts both the OH and a methyl branch on C2: 2-methylpentan-2-ol (a tertiary alcohol).

C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CONHCH<sub>3</sub> contains a phenyl ring attached to –CONH–, which is an amide group (C=O bonded to N). The C=O is part of the amide, so it is not counted separately as a carbonyl or amine.

Butan-2-ol has a chiral carbon (bonded to H, OH, CH<sub>3</sub> and C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>), so it exists as two optical isomers (enantiomers). But-1-ene/but-2-ene and butan-1-ol/butan-2-ol are structural isomers, and but-1-ene has no cis/trans isomers.

C3 in CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CHBr–CH<sub>3</sub> has four different groups (H, Br, CH<sub>3</sub>, CH=CH<sub>2</sub>), so it is chiral (optical isomers). There is no geometric isomerism because the terminal carbon of the C=C carries two identical H atoms.

The longest chain containing the C=C runs through the CH2CH3 branch: 6 carbons, hexene. Numbering from the end nearer the double bond puts it at C2 with methyls on C2 and C4: 2,4-dimethylhex-2-ene. The other names use too short a chain.

Geometric (cis/trans) isomers have the same groups arranged differently about a C=C. D shows cis- and trans-but-2-ene. C shows the same molecule (propene) drawn twice; A shows structural isomers; B shows the same molecule rotated about a single bond (no restricted rotation).
Aspirin contains a carboxylic acid group (–COOH) on the ring and an ester group (–O–CO–CH3). There is no alcohol –OH and no ketone.
CH3CH(CH3)CONH2 is an amide (–CONH2). The chain of three carbons including the CONH2 carbon (C1) carries a methyl on C2: 2-methylpropanamide.
The isomers are 1,1-dichlorocyclobutane, cis- and trans-1,2-dichlorocyclobutane, and cis- and trans-1,3-dichlorocyclobutane: 5. The ring prevents rotation, which creates the cis/trans pairs.
p1.flag: No markscheme; trans-1,2 is also chiral, so counting enantiomers gives 6 (D)

p1.key: Successive members of a homologous series share the same functional group, so they have similar chemical properties and the same general formula, and each differs from the next by –CH2–.
Propanenitrile has three carbons including the –C≡N carbon: CH3CH2CN. B is butanenitrile; C and D are amines.
p1.flag: Nitriles not in 2025 guide functional groups list

p1.key: In the cis isomer both Cl atoms are on the same side of the ring (A). The geometric isomer is trans, with Cl atoms on opposite sides of the ring plane: C. B is 1,1-dichloro and D is a cyclopropene, so these are different compounds.
Alkynes contain one C≡C triple bond, which means 4 fewer H atoms than the alkane, CnH2n+2: CnH2n−2. CnH2n is alkenes and CnH2n+2 is alkanes.

In butan-2-ol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, C2 has four different groups (H, OH, CH<sub>3</sub>, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>), so it is chiral. The others have no carbon bearing four different groups.
IHD = (2C + 2 + N − H − X)/2. For C4H9N: (8 + 2 + 1 − 9)/2 = 1. C6H6 = 4, C2Cl2 = 2, C2H6O = 0.

X-ray crystallography uses diffraction from the regular lattice of a crystal to locate atoms precisely, giving bond lengths and angles. IR identifies bonds, MS gives molar mass and fragments, and NMR gives hydrogen environments.
The molecule has an –OH group (hydroxyl) and C–O–C linkages (ether: the CH3O– group and the ring O). There is no C=O, so no ester. "Hydroxide" is the OH− ion, not an organic functional group.

Enantiomers have identical physical properties such as melting and boiling points. They rotate plane-polarized light by the same angle in opposite directions, a racemic mixture is optically inactive, and they can react differently with other chiral molecules.

The molecular ion is the whole molecule minus one electron, so its m/z equals the relative molecular mass. It has the largest m/z (not the smallest), and it is often not the most intense or most stable peak.
All 12 H atoms in Si(CH3)4 are in one chemical environment, giving a single strong signal used as the zero reference (δ = 0). It is also inert and volatile (low boiling point).
Aspirin has a –COOH group (carboxyl) and a –O–CO–CH3 group (ester). The O bonded to the ring is part of the ester linkage, not an ether, because it is attached to a C=O.
A tertiary amine has N bonded to three carbon atoms: C3H7N(CH3)2. (CH3)2NH is secondary, C6H5NH2 is primary, and (C2H5)4N+ is a quaternary ammonium ion.
Each signal in a 1H NMR spectrum corresponds to a different chemical environment of hydrogen. Bonds are found by IR and molecular mass by mass spectrometry.
In 2-chlorobutane, C2 carries four different groups (H, Cl, CH3, C2H5), so it is a chiral centre. The other molecules have no carbon bonded to four different groups.
X-ray crystallography maps electron density in a crystal, giving precise bond lengths and angles. IR identifies bonds, MS gives molar mass and fragments, and NMR gives hydrogen environments.
Paracetamol has an –OH on the ring (hydroxyl, a phenol) and an –NH–CO– group (amide). There is no –COOH, no –NH2 (amino) and no C≡N (nitrile).
A secondary carbon is bonded to two other carbons. In CH3CH(Cl)CH(CH3)2, the C carrying Cl is bonded to two carbons, so it is secondary. In B and D the C–Cl carbon is primary; in C it is tertiary.
Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images that always rotate plane-polarized light (in opposite directions). Cis–trans, E/Z and conformational isomers are not necessarily chiral.
A single peak means all the hydrogen atoms are in one chemical environment. It does not mean there is only one H atom (e.g. TMS or benzene have many equivalent H atoms).

X-ray crystallography maps electron density in a crystal, giving precise bond lengths and angles. NMR, IR and mass spectrometry give hydrogen environments, bonds present and molar mass/fragments respectively.
The longest chain is 4 C; the C bearing both OH and a CH3 is C2 (numbering to give OH the lowest locant): 2-methylbutan-2-ol, (CH3)2C(OH)CH2CH3. "2-ethylpropan" ignores the longest chain.
Isoleucine has two chiral centres (the C bearing NH2 and the C bearing CH3), each with four different groups. The maximum number of optical isomers is 22 = 4.
Four signals: ~3.6 (CH2–O), ~3.0 (OH singlet), ~1.6 (CH2) and ~0.9 (CH3 triplet) match CH3CH2CH2OH. Ethanol would give 3 signals; ethoxyethane and propane only 2.
In B, the C bearing OH is bonded to two other carbons (3-methylbutan-2-ol), so it is secondary. A and C have OH on a CH2 (primary); in D the C–OH carbon is bonded to three carbons (tertiary).
Br outranks Cl on C1, and CH2CH3 outranks H on C2. The higher-priority groups (Br and ethyl) are on the same side, so it is Z; the longest chain containing C=C has 4 C: Z-1-bromo-1-chlorobut-1-ene.
In CH3CH2CHBrCH3 (2-bromobutane), C2 has four different groups (H, Br, CH3, C2H5): a chiral carbon. In A, C3 has two identical ethyl groups; C and D have no carbon with four different groups.
IHD = (number of rings) + (number of π bonds). 3-methylcyclohexene has one ring and one C=C: IHD = 2. Check via formula C7H12: (2 × 7 + 2 − 12) ÷ 2 = 2.
Pentan-3-ol, (CH3CH2)2CHOH, is symmetrical: two equivalent CH3 (6H), two equivalent CH2 (4H), one CH (1H) and one OH (1H): 6 : 4 : 1 : 1.

<sup>1</sup>H NMR clearly distinguishes them: propan-1-ol has 4 signals, propan-2-ol only 3 (with a 6H doublet). Both are oxidized by dichromate (same colour change), and they have the same molecular mass and composition.

CH≡CCH2CH3 and CH≡CCH2CH2CH3 are both alkynes with the same functional group and differ by one CH2, so they are in the same homologous series. The other pairs mix functional groups: alcohol/ether, alkene/alkane, ketone/ether.

The structure is (CH3)2CH–CH2–COOH. The longest chain including the COOH carbon has 4 C (butanoic acid), with a methyl group on C3: 3-methylbutanoic acid. "Dimethylpropanoic" names do not use the longest chain.

Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures. I (ethanol/methoxymethane, C2H6O) and III (ethanoic acid/methyl methanoate, C2H4O2) are isomers. In II both formulas describe ethanol, so they are the same compound.
Non-superimposable mirror images are enantiomers (optical isomers), formed by molecules with a chiral centre. Cis–trans isomers and other diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images.

PTFE contains no hydrogen, so its spectrum is the one with no C–H stretching absorption near 2850–3000 cm−1 and strong C–F absorptions around 1000–1400 cm−1. The other three polymers all show strong C–H peaks.

p1.key: In (CH3)2CH–CHCl–CHBr–CH3, the CHCl carbon (H, Cl, isopropyl, CHBrCH3) and the CHBr carbon (H, Br, CH3, CHCl–) each have four different groups: 2 chiral centres. The CH of the isopropyl group carries two identical CH3 groups.
2-Methylbutane is (CH3)2CH–CH2–CH3. It has four H environments: two equivalent CH3 (6H), CH (1H), CH2 (2H), terminal CH3 (3H), giving a ratio of 6 : 1 : 2 : 3.

X-ray crystallography maps electron density in a crystal, giving the positions of atoms and therefore bond lengths and angles. NMR, IR and mass spectrometry identify environments, bonds and fragments but do not measure bond lengths.

The longest chain has 5 carbons (through the ethyl group): CH3CHBr–CH(CH3)–CH2CH3. Numbering from the Br end gives Br on C2 and methyl on C3; substituents go in alphabetical order: 2-bromo-3-methylpentane.

1,2-Dimethylcyclobutane has restricted rotation in the ring, and each substituted ring carbon has two different groups (CH3 and H), so the methyls can be on the same side or opposite sides: cis/trans. A and B each have one alkene carbon with two identical groups, and cyclobutene has no substituents.

IR absorptions match the vibrations of particular bonds, so they identify functional groups (e.g. C=O, O–H). Molar mass comes from mass spectrometry, and 3-D structure and bond angles come from X-ray crystallography.

Options B–D are all C5H12 isomers (hexane in A is larger). 2,2-Dimethylpropane is the most branched and nearly spherical, so it has the smallest surface contact and weakest London forces, and therefore the lowest b.p.
The longest chain is 6 carbons (CH3CH2–CH–CH–CH2CH3), with methyl groups on C3 and C4: 3,4-dimethylhexane. The other names do not use the longest chain.

CHBr=CHBr has restricted rotation about C=C, and each carbon carries two different groups (H and Br), so cis and trans isomers exist. A and B each have a carbon with two identical groups, and C has free rotation about a single bond.

IR absorption bands come from the vibrations of particular bonds, so the spectrum shows which bonds (functional groups) are present. The number of H environments and H ratios come from 1H NMR, and molar mass from mass spectrometry.
In mass spectrometry the molecule is ionized and the molecular ion breaks up into fragments, which means breaking covalent bonds. IR, NMR and X-ray crystallography leave the molecule intact.
C5H12, C7H16 and C8H18 all fit CnH2n+2 (alkanes). C6H12 fits CnH2n (an alkene or cycloalkane), so it belongs to a different series.

CH3CH2CH(CH3)Br (2-bromobutane) has a carbon bonded to four different groups (H, Br, CH3, C2H5), so it is chiral and optically active. In B the CHBr carbon carries two identical ethyl groups, and in C the carbon carries two CH3 groups.
All 12 H atoms in TMS are equivalent, so there is a single peak at 0 ppm. TMS is the reference standard that defines δ = 0. D is a single peak at about 7.3 ppm, which is typical of benzene.
The longest chain includes the ethyl group: six carbons (hexane), with methyl groups on C2 and C4 numbering from the left → 2,4-dimethylhexane. Names C and D don't use the longest chain.

1,2-Dichlorocyclohexane has two ring carbons each with Cl and H; the ring stops rotation so the Cl atoms can be on the same side (cis) or opposite sides (trans). A and B have two identical groups on one C=C carbon; in C the double bond is inside a six-membered ring.

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHClCH<sub>3</sub> (2-chlorobutane) has a chiral carbon bonded to H, Cl, CH<sub>3</sub> and C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>, so it is optically active. In D the central carbon carries two CH<sub>3</sub> groups, so it is not chiral.

All three work: M<sub>r</sub> differs (60 vs 58) so the mass spectra differ; IR shows O–H in propan-2-ol but C=O in propanal; <sup>1</sup>H NMR shows 3 environments for both but different shifts and ratios (6:1:1 vs 3:2:1).
Splitting follows the n + 1 rule: a signal split into n + 1 peaks means there are n hydrogen atoms on the adjacent atom(s). The number of H in an environment comes from the integration (D).

C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub>, C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>4</sub>, C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>6</sub> share the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n−2</sub> and differ by CH<sub>2</sub> each time (alkynes). The other sets do not differ by CH<sub>2</sub>.
The molecule is symmetrical: all four CH2 groups (next to O and to the C=C) are in the same environment and there are no other H atoms, so there is only one signal.
Si(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub> has 12 equivalent H atoms giving one intense signal (why TMS is the reference). (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CH has 9 equivalent H and benzene 6.

p1.key: B (methyl benzoate) has a benzene ring and an ester group –COO–CH<sub>3</sub>. A is a carboxylic acid (benzoic acid); C is an ester without a benzene ring.
The longest chain is four carbons; the OH and one methyl are on C2 and another methyl is on C3: (CH3)2C(OH)CH(CH3)2 = 2,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol.
A racemate contains equal amounts of the two enantiomers, which rotate plane-polarized light equally in opposite directions, so the net rotation is 0°.
X-ray crystallography gives the positions of atoms in a crystal, so bond lengths and angles can be measured. NMR, IR and MS give information on environments, bonds/functional groups and mass.
